They have gone above what you asked for and your client has not moved. So let me ask the useful question. What would have to be in that room for her to sign?
Someone saying that it happened. Not that they are sorry she feels this way. That it happened. She wishes somebody had acknowledged it two years ago, and nobody ever has.
You know they will not put that in writing. Their lawyer will read it as an admission and they will refuse.

Then let us not write it. Let them say it in the room, with you present, and let the agreement say only what the agreement has to say. That way nobody has to sign anything that looks like a climbdown.
That could work. I wish you had said that before lunch, because we spent two hours on a number that was never the difficulty.
So do I. I wish I had said it this morning, and I did not, because I thought the money would be enough. It never was.
Nobody in these rooms works that out on the first attempt. I will go and give them a way to save face, because they will need one.
Thank you. And Marcus, before you go — how often does the thing that unlocks a room turn out not to be money?
She wishes somebody had acknowledged it two years ago.
I wish they would stop treating an acknowledgement as an admission.
I wish I could give you an answer today, and I cannot.
If only somebody had asked her in the first month.

There are six words that ruin an apology and I hear them in almost every room. I am sorry you feel that way. Listen to what that sentence actually does. It moves the problem out of the speaker and into the other person, so what the room hears is that the feeling is the mistake. I have watched a settlement die on those six words, twice, after the money had already been agreed. A working apology has three parts, and it is not complicated. Name what happened. Say what should have happened instead. And give one concrete thing that will be different from now on. That is it. Nothing about intentions, nothing about how difficult it has been for everybody. And a word about the lawyers who tell their clients never to apologise under any circumstances. I understand where that comes from, and I think they are protecting against a risk that is smaller than they believe. In a mediation, what is said in the room cannot be used later, which is a fact that half the people in the room do not know when they walk in. So I tell them. And then I watch somebody say a true sentence out loud for the first time in two years.

Everybody assumed I wanted money. Every meeting was built around a figure, and every time it went up I felt further away from what I was there for, which nobody could understand and I could not explain either, not for a long time. What I wanted was for one person on that side to say out loud that it had happened. Not that they were sorry I was upset. That it happened. It took me eighteen months to be able to say that sentence, and by then everybody had decided I was being difficult about the number. Those two years cost me more than the money ever would have, and I mean that in the ordinary way: my work, my sleep, two friendships. I wish somebody had asked me, in the first month, what I was actually asking for. Nobody did. And I want to be fair about my own lawyer, because he was very good and he never asked me either. I do not think anybody had taught him that it was a question you could ask. I do not blame him for it. I do wish that somebody had taught him.

The problem these laws exist to solve is a strange one. The people best placed to apologise are almost always the people whose own lawyers have told them, correctly under the old rules, that anything they say can be produced in court later and read back to them by somebody who is not on their side. So the apology does not happen, and the case that could have ended in a conversation runs for three years instead. An apology law makes the statement inadmissible: it cannot be used as evidence of liability, which means it can finally be given. Where these laws have been introduced, the number of claims has fallen, and the researchers have been careful about explaining why, because falling numbers can mean several things. The explanation that has held up best is also the simplest. A large share of those claims were never really about money. There is a limit, and the study that everybody quotes is blunt about it. A protected apology only works if the person receiving it believes it. A begrudging one, offered because a lawyer has just explained that it is now safe to offer, makes the outcome measurably worse than saying nothing at all.
